answers.question: List of scenarios
answers.answer: Three scenarios were used: 1) Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Category), 2) Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category), and 3) Current Policies (Hot House World Category). These are based on Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios.
answers.evidence: "The sector group chose the following three Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios as the basis for the sector-level scenarios: Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Category), Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category), Current Policies (Hot House World Category)"
answers.location_hint: Page 2 of Climate-Related Disclosures / Page 24 of Annual Report
answers.notes: The three scenarios are clearly listed in a table with descriptions. Net Zero 2050 limits warming to 1.6°C by 2050 (reducing to 1.4°C by 2100); Delayed Transition limits warming to 1.7°C by 2050 (reducing to 1.6°C by 2100); Current Policies results in 2°C by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100.

answers.question: Global temperature outcome by 2100
answers.answer:
The three scenarios project the following global temperature outcomes by 2100:
1. Net Zero 2050 (Orderly): 1.4°C by 2100
2. Delayed Transition (Disorderly): 1.6°C by 2100
3. Current Policies (Hot House World): more than 3°C by 2100

answers.question: Customised scenarios
answers.answer: Yes. Briscoe Group collaborated with other retail industry participants to co-design a set of integrated climate change scenarios for New Zealand's retail sector. The sector group chose three Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS)-based scenarios: a baseline representing 1.1°C of global warming, and two further scenarios representing 1.5°C (using a mixture of Orderly and Disorderly Transition narratives) and 3.0°C (Hothouse World) of global warming.
answers.evidence: "In the first half of the year, we collaborated with other retail industry participants to co-design a set of integrated climate change scenarios for New Zealand's retail sector. The sector group chose the following three Network for Greening the [Financial System scenarios]... an initial risk screening of a master list of over 30 risks and opportunities, a baseline risk assessment representing 1.1°C of global warming helping us to identify the current physical and transition impacts we have incurred, and two further scenarios representing 1.5°C and 3.0°C of global warming."
answers.location_hint: Briscoe Group 2024 Annual Report, page 24; Climate-Related Disclosures, page 3
answers.notes: The scenarios were co-designed with retail sector peers and are sector-customised adaptations of NGFS scenarios (Orderly, Disorderly, and Hothouse World), tailored for New Zealand's retail context. The 1.5°C scenario blended Orderly and Disorderly Transition narratives; the 3.0°C scenario used the Hothouse World narrative.

answers.answer: The baseline scenario represents 1.1°C of global warming, helping to identify the current physical and transition impacts incurred. The three NGFS-based scenarios used are: (1) Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Category) — limiting warming to 1.6°C in 2050; (2) Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category) — limiting warming to 1.7°C in 2050; and (3) Current Policies (Hot House World Category) — resulting in 2°C by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100.

answers.question: Damage from acute physical risk considered
answers.answer: Yes. Briscoe Group considers damage from acute physical risks including: increased storminess/extreme winds, river and pluvial flooding, and global supply chain disruption from storms/floods. These risks are identified as causing potential store closures, delays in supply chain, team and customers unable to get to stores, loss of sales and decrease in profit, cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings, increased lease costs, and increased supply chain costs.
answers.evidence: "Increase in storminess (frequency, intensity) including tropical cyclones. Changes in extreme wind speed. Increase in convective weather events (tornadoes, lightning). Changes in extremes: high intensity and persistence of rainfall. Increase in hail severity or frequency. There will be an increasing incidence of storm events with increasing severity impacting supply chains and operations. Potential store closures. Delays in supply chain. Team and customers unable to get to our stores. Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings. Increased lease costs. Increased supply chain costs."
answers.location_hint: Briscoe Group 2024 Annual Report, page 25; Climate-Related Disclosures 2024, page 3
answers.notes: Acute physical risks explicitly identified include increased storminess/extreme winds, river and pluvial flooding, and international port disruption from storms/floods. Sea-level rise is also considered as a chronic physical risk.

answers.question: Non-temperature variables in scenarios
answers.answer: The scenarios include non-temperature variables such as: sea level rise (specifically 0.32m), changes in rainfall extremes (high intensity and persistence), increased storminess/extreme winds (frequency and intensity of tropical cyclones, tornadoes, lightning, hail), river and pluvial flooding, relative sea-level rise (including land movement), change in tidal range or increased water depth, permanent increase in spring high-tide inundation, and rising groundwater from sea-level rise. On the transition side, variables include regulatory/legal interventions, consumer sentiment, and macro-economic conditions.
answers.evidence: "Sea level rise of 0.32m could impact specific locations and increase losses due to flooding." / "Changes in extremes: high intensity and persistence of rainfall. Increase in hail severity or frequency." / "Relative sea-level rise (including land movement). Change in tidal range or increased water depth. Permanent increase in spring high-tide inundation. Rising groundwater from sea-level rise." / "physical impacts are the most severe, as is the financial impact of supply chain disruptions. Transitional impacts are limited as regulation is either not developed or severely delayed."
answers.location_hint: Briscoe Group 2024 Climate-Related Disclosures, pages 3-5; Annual Report pages 25-27
answers.notes: The document explicitly mentions sea level rise of 0.32m as a specific quantified non-temperature variable. Other physical variables (rainfall, wind, flooding) are described qualitatively. Transition variables such as regulatory timing, consumer sentiment, and macro-economic conditions are also referenced in scenario narratives.

answers.question: Scale of scenarios
answers.answer: Briscoe Group used three NGFS-based scenarios at the sector level: (1) Net Zero 2050 (Orderly) — limiting warming to 1.6°C in 2050 / 1.4°C by 2100; (2) Delayed Transition (Disorderly) — limiting warming to 1.7°C in 2050 / 1.6°C by 2100; (3) Current Policies (Hothouse World) — resulting in 2°C by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100. These were also mapped to entity-level warming benchmarks of 1.1°C (baseline), 1.5°C, and 3.0°C for the risk assessment workshops.

Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category): limit global warming to 1.7°C in 2050 and reducing to 1.6°C by 2100. Current Policies (Hot House World Category): resulting in 2°C global warming by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100." and "a baseline risk assessment representing 1.1°C of global warming... and two further scenarios representing 1.5°C and 3.0°C of global warming."
answers.notes: Three NGFS scenarios were used at sector level, with entity-level risk assessment conducted at 1.1°C (baseline), 1.5°C, and 3.0°C warming levels.

answers.question: Time frames
answers.answer:
Briscoe Group uses three time horizons in its climate-related risk assessment:
- Short-term: one to three years
- Medium-term: three to 10 years
- Long-term: more than 10 years

For scenario analysis, three broader time horizons were also considered: short (2023–2030), medium (2031–2040), and long (2041–2050).
answers.evidence: "The time horizons utilised in the climate-risk assessment process were: • Short-term: one to three years • Medium-term: three to 10 years • Long term: > 10years" and "These scenarios considered three different time horizons: short (2023-2030), medium (2031-2040) and long (2041-2050)"
answers.location_hint: Climate-Related Disclosures, Risk Management section (p.5); Scenario Analysis section (p.2/p.24)
answers.notes: The entity-level business planning time horizons (1–3 years, 3–10 years, >10 years) were used for ranking risks and opportunities, while the sector-based scenario horizons (2023–2030, 2031–2040, 2041–2050) provided broader guidance in workshops.

answers.question: Justification for scenario/model choice
answers.answer: Briscoe Group used three NGFS (Network for Greening the Financial System) scenarios — Net Zero 2050 (Orderly), Delayed Transition (Disorderly), and Current Policies (Hot House World) — co-designed with other retail industry participants for New Zealand's retail sector. Using a combination of scenarios was intended to add resilience to the risk assessment process and the resultant strategy, as the company prepares for inevitable uncertainty in the short to medium-term. The scenarios cover a range of warming outcomes (1.5°C to 3°C+) and transition pathways, allowing assessment of both physical and transition-related risks across short, medium, and long-term horizons.
answers.evidence: "In the first half of the year, we collaborated with other retail industry participants to co-design a set of integrated climate change scenarios for New Zealand's retail sector. The sector group chose the following three Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios as the basis for the sector-level scenarios... Using a combination of scenarios was intended to add resilience to the risk assessment process and the resultant strategy as we prepare for inevitable uncertainty in the short to medium-term."
answers.location_hint: Briscoe Group 2024 Annual Report, page 24-25; Climate-Related Disclosures, page 2-3
answers.notes: The justification explicitly states that using a combination of scenarios adds resilience to the risk assessment process. The NGFS scenarios were chosen collaboratively with retail industry peers and adapted into retail sector narratives covering three time horizons.

answers.question: Historic climate impacts
answers.answer: Briscoe Group has experienced some historic climate impacts, though physical impacts have not significantly affected operations. These include: increased insurance premiums off the back of climate-related events occurring in NZ, increased legislation (specifically the newly introduced NZ Climate related disclosures), and severe weather events impacting team members particularly in Hastings, Napier, Gisborne and parts of Auckland.
answers.evidence: "Although we have started to feel the transitional impacts of climate change on our business relating to increased legislation (specifically the newly introduced NZ Climate related disclosures) and have seen an increase in insurance premiums off the back of climate-related events occurring in NZ, we have been fortunate that the physical impacts experienced by our business have not significantly impacted operations. We are cognisant some of our team members particularly in Hastings, Napier, Gisborne and parts of Auckland felt the impacts of the severe weather events earlier in the year and we are proud of how our Management team responded to provide support to those impacted, and the way in which our team members worked to ensure our impacted stores could remain open."
answers.location_hint: Page 24 of Annual Report / Page 2 of Climate-Related Disclosures
answers.notes: The document also references a baseline risk assessment at 1.1°C of global warming to identify current physical and transition impacts incurred, but specific quantified historic financial impacts are not disclosed.

answers.question: Direct and indirect physical climate risks
answers.answer:
Briscoe Group identifies the following key physical climate risks:

1. **Sustainable Sourcing (indirect/supply chain):** Climate-related events increasing globally impact the availability of raw materials for suppliers, affecting the availability of products. Potential financial impacts include decreased ability to purchase required inventory levels, increased cost of inventory, and decreased margin/profit. Business response: diversification of product range and working with suppliers to ensure diversity in product ranges and sustainable sourcing.

2. **Increased storminess / extreme winds / river and pluvial flooding (direct and indirect):** Increasing frequency and intensity of storm events (including tropical cyclones, extreme winds, convective weather events, high-intensity rainfall, hail) impacting supply chains and operations. Potential impacts include potential store closures, delays in supply chain, and team/customers unable to get to stores. Financial impacts include loss of sales, decreased profit, cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings, increased lease costs, and increased supply chain costs. Business response: transition planning to ensure resilience to extreme weather events.

3. **Global supply chain risk (indirect):** A main international port affected by storms or floods, making it unable to get goods to New Zealand, requiring sourcing from alternative locations, and causing supply chain delays. Financial impacts include loss of sales, decreased profit, and increased supply chain costs. Business response: transition planning to build resilience into supply chain.
answers.evidence: "KEY PHYSICAL RISKS: Sustainable Sourcing – With climate-related events increasing globally, this is a significant risk to those who want to source sustainable products. Impact of a changing climate on the availability of raw materials for our suppliers. Availability of products offered to us from our suppliers. Decreased ability to purchase required levels of inventory. Diversification of product range. Increased cost of inventory. Decrease in margin/profit. Working with suppliers to ensure diversity in product ranges and that products are sourced sustainably. Increased storminess/ extreme winds / River and pluvial flooding – Increase in storminess (frequency, intensity) including tropical cyclones. Changes in extreme wind speed. Increase in convective weather events (tornadoes, lightning). Changes in extremes: high intensity and persistence of rainfall. Increase in hail severity or frequency. There will be an increasing incidence of storm events with increasing severity impacting supply chains and operations. Potential store closures. Delays in supply chain. Team and customers unable to get to our stores. Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings. Increased lease costs. Increased supply chain costs. Transition planning to ensure resilience to extreme weather events. Global supply chain risk – A main international port is affected (e.g. by storms/or floods). Unable to get goods to New Zealand. Need to source goods from alternative location. Delays in supply chain. Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Increased supply chain costs. Transition planning to build resilience into supply chain."
answers.location_hint: Annual Report 2024, p.25; Climate-Related Disclosures 2024, p.3
answers.notes: The document distinguishes between direct physical risks (storminess/flooding affecting stores and operations) and indirect physical risks (sustainable sourcing and global supply chain disruption due to climate events affecting suppliers and ports).
